response_shapes.ok_filtered: Authorized response with hidden elements omitted
response_shapes.omitted: Item absent; no placeholder, count, or hint
response_shapes.not_found: Indistinguishable not-found (same status, body shape, headers, and timing envelope as nonexistent)
response_shapes.forbidden: Known-limited permission on a readable resource (ST-42)
response_shapes.conflict_filtered: Conflict response without unreadable current values
response_shapes.validation_generic: Generic validation error naming only the caller's own input
response_shapes.step_up_required: Fresh step-up proof required; nothing executed and no resource information beyond the challenge

threats.description: ID substitution: a request names a record, brand, or project ID from another workspace.
Background job or webhook processed under the wrong workspace context.
Read a hidden record through its parent, child, or breadcrumb.
Discover a hidden record through a dependency, related link, or derived Blocked condition.
Read hidden content through mentions, activity, or notifications.
Fetch hidden files through attachment URLs, signed URLs, or file version IDs.
Obtain hidden records through export, report delivery, or webhooks.
Retrieve hidden records through search, AI answers, citations, or recommendations.
Infer hidden records from counts, facets, pagination totals, capacity, or metric totals.
Distinguish nonexistent from unauthorized by status code, error text, timing, or uniqueness errors.
Use filters or sorts on hidden fields or hidden relationships as an oracle.
Brand member reads a restricted project's tasks through brand-level grants or brand-wide views.
Owner/admin silently reads a sensitive brand without elevation.
Continue access after share expiry or revocation (cached pages, SSE, notifications, search).
Use a revoked or expired token, session, or OAuth consent.
Gain access by being added to a team that holds grants the adder cannot grant; or keep access after removal from a team.
Read a hidden field through a calculated field, conflict response, audit history, export, notification, search snippet, or AI.
A queued job or long-running agent acts with permissions that were revoked after enqueue.
A cached derived condition or projection serves a stale authorization decision.
Guest reshares, sees unshared children/parents, the member directory, or all-brands aggregates.
Guest reaches trash or archived content of formerly shared records.
Agent reads or acts outside its run scope (prompt-injected scope expansion).
Confused deputy: low-privilege user assigns a task to a powerful agent or automation to reach data they cannot read.
Agent, automation, or AI approves its own output or performs gated actions without approval.
Forged inbound webhook or replayed provider event creates or modifies records.
Integration writes outside its mapped brand/project scope or exfiltrates via outbound sync.
Platform support reads tenant data without a valid support grant or impersonates a user.
Workspace admin exports or views data outside their authority or without audit.
Departed member retains access via sessions, personal tokens, OAuth clients, automations, or running agents.
Last owner removed or ownership transfer escalates a non-owner.
Pooled connection reuses another tenant's context or runs without context.
Worker or maintenance role bypasses RLS broadly.
Not-found versus forbidden difference reveals that a readable record exists but an action is forbidden — acceptable only for readable records.
Client supplies a brand, role, plan, actor, or approval field to bypass checks.
Account takeover through account security: a stolen or unattended session, or a delegated credential, enrolls or disables a second factor or regenerates recovery codes.

Tenant-creation abuse: a delegated or non-human principal, an unverified or deleted account, a flood of requests, or a replayed request creates workspaces or gains tenant authority through creation, or a body claim names an existing workspace, role, or membership.

Invitation abuse: replaying, forwarding, or racing an invitation token; accepting with a different account; enumerating accounts or memberships through invite outcomes; a guest invitation conferring workspace, brand, or inherited access; an administrator inviting an owner.

Ownership or departure failure: a workspace left without an active owner, an ownership transfer accepted by the wrong principal or without step-up, a removed or suspended member keeping access through sessions, cached contexts, teams, grants, queued jobs, or pooled connections, or owned resources left without an accountable owner.

Personal navigation leakage: favorites, recents, view state, URL scope, breadcrumbs, page titles, palette results, shortcuts, or navigation entries revealing or re-opening a record, brand, person, or destination the viewer can no longer (or never could) access, including through forged identifiers, stale client caches, stored state, or another workspace's identifiers.

Task exposure through responsibility or sharing: assignees, creators, or labels gaining access; a task share exposing its parent, project, children, relationships, links to inaccessible records, history, or brand aggregates; hidden relationship endpoints or descendants affecting counts, completion overrides, or rollups.

Workflow and field exposure: custom statuses, transitions, or approvals bypassing category, Complete/Reopen, or required-field rules; approvers or person/label field values gaining access; hidden fields, options, or formula inputs leaking through payloads, errors, counts, sorting, serialization, audit, or formula results; stale approvals or previews replayed.

Task interaction exposure: freshness, blocked, missing-data, or duplicate signals, bulk previews and reports, undo entries, reminders, snoozes, template applications, or recurring occurrences revealing unreadable tasks, hidden fields, or other people's personal state, by content, count, error, or timing; recurrence or bulk acting beyond current authority.

Capture exposure: another person's Inbox items or notes visible to anyone (including owners and administrators); parsing, previews, counts, errors, or timing revealing hidden brands, projects, members, or labels; triage or note conversion creating work where the person lacks record.create; intake forms leaking the queue or accepting submissions from people who cannot read the brand; rate and size bounds bypassed.

Saved-view exposure: a shared, pinned, or default view widening record access; rows, totals, group counts, group labels, cursors, filter-value labels, exports, or timing revealing hidden records, brands, projects, members, labels, or fields; personal views visible to others (including owners and administrators); sharing, pinning, or defaults set without authority at the exact scope; a cursor or export reused by another person or after revocation.

Time exposure and tampering: entries, totals, reports, timesheets, approval views, or exports naming or counting work the viewer cannot read; logging, editing, or moving time without time.log_own on the work; changing another person's entries; approving a brand line without manage now, without seeing all of it, or as a self-approval the policy forbids; unlocking an approved period without workspace admin authority, a reason, or step-up; editing or moving submitted or approved time through any path.

Core view exposure: a board column count, calendar event, timeline or Gantt bar, dependency arrow, workload total, milestone, portfolio percentage, timesheet cell, or activity entry revealing a record, endpoint, field, or person the viewer cannot read; board moves or date changes bypassing workflow gates, permissions, or versions, or silently changing deadlines; activity readable through a share; another person's time shown.

Planning exposure and drift: another person's Today, blocks, series, or records visible to anyone; commitments or blocks revealing or granting access to tasks the owner cannot read (including after revocation); Today lists counting hidden work; planning commands changing due dates or deadlines; locked items or focus blocks moved or overlapped; daily records rewritten.

Cross-brand capacity leakage: another person's capacity, reservations, or conflicts visible without capacity.view; time-off kinds, labels, or entries visible to anyone but their owner; blocks, estimates, holidays, or conflicts revealing work or brands the viewer cannot read; reservations set without capacity.reserve; visibility outliving a revoked grant.

Collaboration leakage and tampering: comments, replies, reactions, mentions, followers, review requests and decisions, delegation, or assignment history revealing a record, person, team, field, or prior value the viewer cannot read, through lists, counts, chips, mention pickers, the Following view, queues, or activity; mentions or reviewer lists confirming hidden people; another person's comment edited or rewritten (administrators included); edits or deletions outside the author's window; decisions made by non-reviewers, on a changed version, twice, or by the requester against the self-approval policy; following inherited from role, assignment, or share; a delegation that grants access or names hidden people; comment text surviving in audit or after purge.

Notification leakage and tampering: notifications, digests, email, browser alerts, search, counts, delivery history, or failure messages revealing a record title, person, brand, project, count, or prior value the recipient cannot read now (after revocation, deletion, departure, a sensitive brand, or a guest share ending); another person's notification, state, preference, profile, or delivery read or changed; a notice created for someone who cannot read the record; preferences, mutes, quiet hours, or defaults used to hide a permission or share change from its subject or to widen delivery; delivery health or retry reachable without authority; failure messages carrying content or addresses; a delivery reported as delivered when only queued or when no provider is configured; content surviving the purge of its record or the departure of its recipient.

Document leakage and tampering: a document, version, suggestion, reference, backlink, export, notification, or search hit revealing a title, identifier, brand, project, person, embed, comment, or prior value the viewer cannot read now (after revocation, a sensitive brand, a share ending, or a record leaving the viewer's reach); a share reaching the tree, ancestors, or subpages around a document; a stale or forged restricted token restoring or exposing a reference; a content save overwriting a newer version, or an old version rewritten or deleted; a suggestion applied to a block that changed, or made to change access; a link to a record the author could not read; backlinks naming documents or targets the viewer cannot read; export carrying more than the viewer may read, or content in audit; an AI-source approval outliving the version it names; documents surviving the purge of their placement or the departure of their owner.

File and deliverable leakage and malicious content: a file, version, name, size, preview, comparison, signed URL, upload session, deliverable, or storage figure of a workspace, brand, project, task, or comment the caller cannot read reached through metadata, list, download, preview, compare, deliverable, review queue, or error responses (or told apart from an unknown one); access surviving a revocation beyond the next request; a signed URL that was tampered with, reused for another object or operation, or replayed after its lifetime, or one stored, logged, emitted, or exported; another person's upload session completed or read; a comment attachment added by someone other than its author; a guest reaching workspace-level files; the storage quota bypassed by concurrent uploads; infected, unscanned, or failed-scan bytes downloaded; active content (SVG, HTML, scripts) rendered inline from the application's storage; the server fetching an external link (SSRF); an accepted deliverable's evidence changed, replaced, or purged.

Live editing leakage and bypass: a hidden editor, caret, name, record, reference, or content reached through presence, a snapshot, an operation, an event, or an error (or told apart from an unknown document); a revoked, removed, archived, trashed, or purged document still readable or writable beyond the next request through a session that was already open; a session handle used by someone else; a read-only or guest session that writes; a live operation that appends content outside the document version history, adds a link to a record the editor cannot read, restores a restricted token it never held, or exceeds the document bounds; a plain save, restore, or suggestion that overwrites or discards unsaved live work; presence or cursor traffic that is audited, stored beyond its expiry, or copied into events; a stale session that keeps editing.

Search leakage and bypass: a hidden record's existence, title, text, rank, order, count, facet, excerpt, index state, or timing reached through a query, a page, a cursor, a filter, the palette, a recent search, or opening a result (or told apart from an unknown record); a share, role, brand, project, or lifecycle change that still shows results until the index is rebuilt; a deleted comment or a trashed file found while the index lags; text the owning module would not show (custom field values, live drafts, restricted reference labels) reaching the index; a person's name shown to a viewer who may not see people; a filter naming a hidden brand or project told apart from an unknown one; a cursor, recent search, or index status used by or revealing something to someone else; another workspace searched or opened; a poison record blocking the index, or an incomplete index presented as complete.

Hidden work disclosed through a goal or portfolio aggregate: a count, percentage, progress, health, reason, dependency, budget, effort, deadline, logged-time total, label, or truncation notice that changes with, or names, a brand, project, task, link, or time entry the viewer cannot read (or tells a hidden project from an absent one); progress or health presented as covering work the viewer cannot see; a total that sums across currencies or presents untracked spend or AI usage as measured.

Existence disclosure through links, targets, and portfolio members: a project, task, goal, or portfolio told apart from an unknown one by a different answer when linking, listing, reading, or editing; a link or portfolio member to work the editor cannot read, or in the wrong brand or project, accepted; a hidden member listed, counted, or dropped when an editor saves a portfolio; a link or membership surviving the purge of the work it names.

Goals and portfolios reached by guests and share-only readers: a guest, a share-only reader, or a member without workspace-level read listing, reading, or counting workspace-level or brand goals and portfolios, or obtaining them through a share, a favorite, a recent item, or an error; a goal or portfolio made shareable.

Stale or cached aggregates after access narrows: a figure, label, or link target computed for one viewer shown to another or kept after a grant is revoked, a role changes, a brand is archived, or work is moved or trashed; a stored number derived from linked work that is older than the work; a response that a shared cache or browser may keep.

Forged, tampered, replayed, or flooded progress: a goal whose progress comes from linked work or key results set by hand; a check-in changed or deleted after it was recorded, written by someone who cannot update the goal, on a closed or archived goal, or attributed to someone else; a retried request recorded twice; a flood of check-ins from one member; a stale edit overwriting a newer one.

Goal and portfolio export exfiltration and injection: an export that contains a goal, key result, portfolio, project, or total the exporter cannot read, is unbounded, silently truncated, unaudited, or kept after it is served; a spreadsheet formula, command, or link planted through a title, unit, note, owner name, or project name.

Recalculation poisoning, lease abuse, and cross-workspace job reads: a background sweep that reads or writes another workspace's goals, appends the same computed check-in twice, stores a number that depends on one viewer's access, lets a crashed or slow worker block a goal for ever, lets one failing goal block the others, stores goal text or a free-form error in its state, or discovers work through anything but workspace identifiers; a row that breaks the placement, period, or measurement rules because a command was bypassed.

Orphan findings revealing hidden links: a project reported as unlinked, or a goal as without active work, because of links or work the viewer cannot read (or reported as linked through a goal they cannot see); a finding that names, counts, or hints at a hidden goal, link, project, or task; a finding not labelled as relative to the viewer.

Hidden work disclosed through a metric: a count, percentage, estimate sum, median, percentile, mean, extreme, age band, workload total, breakdown row, order, rank, record total, drill-through item or position, export row, result digest, freshness figure, or timing that changes with, or names, a brand, project, task, deliverable, assignment, time entry, or status history the viewer cannot read (or tells a hidden brand or project from an absent one); a person named to a viewer who may not see people, or an unowned-task count given to one who may not see owners; a cursor used by or revealing something to someone else; another workspace's figures; a figure stored for one viewer and served to another; a revocation, trash, or departure that still shows work until a recomputation.

Forged, concealed, or stale derived history and freshness: a status span written, changed, backdated, or removed outside the task's own transaction to alter cycle time or time in status; a reconciliation that backdates or double-closes a span, runs overlapping on one workspace, acts on another workspace, repairs a purged record, or hides its failure; a figure that presents assumed, repaired, lagging, or failing history as complete, or an unavailable source as zero; a past or future `as_of` that reveals what the viewer could not see then or now or describes the present as the past; an export or digest that differs from the figure it names or carries formula content; unbounded computation by scope or window; an unprivileged person moving the reconciliation schedule.

Dashboard aggregate disclosure: a widget figure, group, breakdown, total, label, truncation or capped-count notice, empty state, or drill-through that includes, counts, or hints at brands, projects, or tasks the viewer cannot read, or a widget whose mere presence or absence reveals a hidden source.

Stale reporting after revocation: a stored or cached metric, a saved dashboard, or a report share that keeps showing figures or records after a grant, share, membership, or role is revoked or expires.

Report share escalation: a share that grants data instead of the saved definition, widens a grantee's access beyond their own, reaches another scope, can be shared onward, lets a guest or share-only reader see workspace or brand totals, or lets a person with only view access create or revoke shares.

Scheduled delivery leak: a report email or run that carries figures computed for another person (the owner or the sender), reaches a recipient who can no longer read it, is sent again or as a backlog, or is sent after its accountable owner lost the authority to schedule it or left.

Export leak: a CSV or PDF export that includes rows, fields, groups, or notes the requester cannot read, executes a formula in a cell, is unbounded, is not audited, or is produced for a person who may not export.

Personal dashboard exposure: an administrator, owner, another member, or a departing member's successor reading, listing, restoring, or counting a personal dashboard that is not theirs; or a personal dashboard whose existence differs from an unknown identifier in status, body, headers, or timing.

Replay and race: a repeated or concurrent create, edit, share, schedule, or delivery that applies twice, loses an edit, sends the same occurrence twice, or lets a second writer overwrite the first without a version conflict.

Misleading or unavailable source: a figure from an unavailable or out-of-date source shown as current or complete, a provider that is not configured reported as a delivered email, or an estimated or incomplete figure shown without saying so.
Credential disclosure: an OAuth token or API key returned, logged, audited, indexed, or left in a row after disconnect or departure.
Connection leak: a connection, sync, or conflict from another brand or workspace is listed or read.
Unauthorized configuration: a guest, read-only member, or member without manage connects, tests, syncs, or disconnects.
Secret survives disconnect or departure: the vault reference remains usable after disconnect, retention removal, or the owner leaving.
Sync applied twice: a repeated idempotency key or delivery advances the checkpoint again or writes the same external identity twice.
Conflict hidden or resolved twice: both sides changed and the conflict is missing, or a resolution applies again.
Unconfigured or degraded provider reported as healthy: a provider that is not configured, or a degraded provider, is shown as connected and its writes are applied.
Scope wider than granted: a connection is stored with a scope the provider does not offer, or a sync writes without the write scope.
A stolen, revoked, expired, or narrowed API token is accepted as the member, or the token secret is returned after it was shown.
A token limited to one brand reads or writes another brand.
An inbound webhook with a bad signature, stale timestamp, or unknown endpoint is treated as authentic or discloses whether the endpoint exists.
An outbound webhook delivers a record the subscription owner can no longer read, or stores a response body.
A replayed write applies twice, or a delivery is dropped instead of retried.

A person's connected calendars, event titles, schedule conflicts, or busy time reach anyone but that person, directly or through derived availability, counts, conflicts, or Today (anonymous free/busy).
A calendar change silently overwrites the person's plan or the provider copy, loops between them, applies after the owner lost authority, or changes a due date or deadline.
A calendar authorization completes with a mismatched state or for someone other than its initiator, or a scope declined at the provider widens the connection.
An unconfigured provider, a test double, an outage, or an invalidated checkpoint is reported as live, current synchronization.

A Phase 6 surface (connection, API token, MCP access, webhook, or import) reaches a workspace, brand, or record its principal cannot read, discloses hidden identifiers through its refusals, or keeps acting after revocation, suspension, removal, or departure.

An AI request sends content outside the initiator's current read access or explicit scope: hidden or unknown records, fields that are not AI-eligible or exceed the workspace data class, restricted brands, brand instructions or free text carrying credentials, or provider keys.

A queued, retried, or replayed AI action keeps dispatching or rendering after the initiator loses access or departs, after the delegating token or consent is revoked, or after the configuration it was authorized against changes; or a repeated Idempotency-Key sends the request again.

AI history, usage administration, exports, or dashboards reveal another person's prompt, output, or context, or reveal content whose sources the reader can no longer read (a generated paraphrase as a backdoor).

AI spending exceeds a configured hard limit through overlapping dispatches, retries, worker loss, unknown outcomes, limit changes, or period rollover; or an unknown cost is shown as zero, or a cancelled, partial, or failed run is shown as a success.

Provider output, model capabilities, or configuration gain authority: output changes records or declares work complete; a real provider receives workspace data without explicit approval, a secret store, or an entitlement; a model is substituted silently; or unconfigured AI is reported as failing or as ready.

AI user content (a rendered prompt, brand instructions, or source-record content) or a key reference survives departure, retention, or account erasure in generic execution storage: a job checkpoint, operation result, attempt detail, outbox payload, or effect ledger, including copies written before a fix, so erasure reports success while a durable copy remains.

A hard spending limit rests on an optimistic assumption: a provider error that may have been charged is settled at zero and retried, a real model's input bound is an unverified estimate, an attempt is priced from the current registry instead of what was confirmed, or invalid or over-bound usage is accepted, clamped, or priced as zero.

Provider stream data gains trust it has not earned: locally clipped text is reported as a complete answer, negative, fractional, unsafe, contradictory, or missing usage or an unsupported stop reason is accepted as success, or an unbounded event or stream exhausts memory while waiting for a separator.

AI retrieval, a context manifest, citations, or derived figures disclose a record the person cannot read or did not choose: a search candidate used without a canonical re-check, an out-of-scope or restricted source sent, or a hidden source revealed through its identifier, type, title, snippet, count, grouping, exclusion detail, availability, timing, history, or error.

Model output gains authority it has not earned: an invented or cross-workspace citation, record identifier, title, link, or approval state becomes a trusted reference; a fabricated quotation is shown as exact; a generated status, completion, cost, date, or result is presented as a fact; or generated markup executes or fetches.

A stale context outlives a change: a preview, queued run, retry, or late provider response uses or publishes sources after access revocation, departure, a version or field-policy or sensitivity change, trash, or erasure; or history, exports, or citations keep a copy of a now-revoked source.

Untrusted input widens AI retrieval: instructions inside a source or question, a client-supplied snippet, title, version, or manifest, or a conflicting scope cause additional retrieval, broader scope, more provider data, or a side effect beyond the person's authorized, explicit choice.

A change the person did not review is applied: a forged, replayed, expired, or stale approval, fingerprint, revision, or selection; an approval by someone else; or client-supplied JSON presented as model output is accepted as authority to change records.

An AI proposal acts beyond the person's authority: it targets records outside its reviewed manifest or another workspace, resolves a foreign or another proposal's temporary reference, changes permissions or deletes, writes domain tables directly, or bypasses workflow approval, required-field, version, cycle, depth, live-edit, lock, or step-up rules.

Applying a proposal misstates or exceeds what happened: it overwrites a target that changed after review, applies after revocation, a policy change, or expiry, commits part of an atomic selection, applies twice under retries, races, or a restart, or reports success for changes that were rolled back or never ran.

Proposal content (proposed values, current before-values, titles, reasons) outlives or escapes its authority: it stays readable after a source becomes unreadable or the data-use policy narrows, survives erasure or departure, or is copied into logs, checkpoints, metrics, events, audit, or exports.

A device-stored copy of proposal content (unsaved edits) outlives the person's authority or session: it is readable to another account in the same browser, survives sign-out, session invalidation, erasure, withholding, or revocation, or is shown again before the server has re-checked access.

A typed AI action is steered beyond its declaration: free text switches the action, widens the scope, names unsupported sources, adds a capability or tool, or a model-supplied identifier, name, label, or member is treated as authority instead of a server-issued choice.

Analysis output fabricates or leaks: an item cites a source outside the manifest, quotes text not in it, claims completion, results, or status the records contradict, or a rule finding counts or names hidden, foreign, or unknown work.

A cost confirmation or clarification is reused for a different request: changed action, instruction, brief, answers, sources, choices, or bounds run on an earlier estimate, or an answered question is applied as a business edit.

Personal calendar or goal context escapes its reader: another member, an administrator, or a broader connection reads a member's mirrored meeting, or a hidden goal's existence is revealed through refusals or drafts.

Choices offered to a drafting action (label names, member display names) leave through a side path: unredacted, unclassified, unlisted for the person, outside the confirmed digest, or surviving in generated content after a choice becomes unavailable or the data-use policy narrows.

A proposal Apply trusts a record as version-checked without holding its row lock (a relationship's other end or a container it only referenced), so a concurrent change committed before the later update is overwritten under an old approval.
A briefing computed for (or cached from) a broader recipient is redistributed to a narrower one, so counts, titles, deltas, or comparisons reveal work the narrower recipient cannot read.
A briefing published before a revocation, trash, or departure keeps showing a record (or a delta that implies it) at display, export, or comparison time.

A scheduled briefing runs twice for one intended local occurrence (DST fold, overlapping sweeps, restart, timeout after commit), runs under a superseded schedule revision, or advances the comparison baseline twice.
A correction note crosses recipients or brands, overrides canonical facts, edits a record, or carries a credential or prompt injection into later briefings or a model.
A briefing notice in the notification centre or email exposes briefing content, or is delivered after the recipient lost access; an unconfigured email channel is reported as delivered.
A departed recipient's schedules keep generating, or their briefing and note content survives erasure, while erasure deletes business records it should keep.

A saved briefing total, comparison, or coverage figure is re-checked only through its displayed sample, so a contributor outside the sample, a previous-window-only contributor, an aggregate without listed rows, or a permission held on another brand keeps a hidden count visible after access is lost (including at notification send time).

A correction note is listed, edited, decided, replayed, or reused after its source evidence became unreadable, so its text, scope, or statement identifier (which may quote protected content) survives the revocation, or it is newly approved without access.

Configured technical retention never discovers a workspace whose expired content is briefings only (no AI runs, or only erased ones), so briefing content outlives its retention period; notes on erased briefings remain a recovery path.

A briefing figure whose evidence basis exceeds the stored bound is kept as a threshold, lower bound, shown count, size flag, or coverage state with an empty basis, so it cannot be re-authorized and keeps describing work the recipient can no longer read.

A capture interpretation or transcript resolves a brand, project, owner, or label the person cannot read, or answers differently for a hidden name than for an unknown one, revealing that hidden work exists.

Model output or instructions inside a capture, transcript, or plan become saved values, records, links, or actions: invented names or dates, spans that are not the person's words, a fetched URL, or an executed instruction.
Raw audio or transcript text escapes the protected content boundary into job arguments, checkpoints, logs, audit, or metrics, or the audio outlives transcription, cancellation, failure, or expiry.

A daily plan approved against an earlier state of the day is applied after time off, holidays, meetings, blocks, Today, or estimates changed, so it overwrites concurrent work or double-books the person.
The planner moves or removes locked commitments or focus blocks, changes task dates, touches another person's blocks, or applies a postponement nobody selected.
Plan totals, coverage, or deferral lists rest on candidates or blockers that are not re-authorized (an empty or sampled basis), so a plan keeps describing work the person can no longer read.
Another person, another workspace, or a delegated bearer caller reaches a plan proposal, an interpretation, or a recording.
An upload claims a format, duration, size, or name it does not have, or a link is fetched, so unbounded or arbitrary content reaches the transcription provider or the queue grows without bound.
Departure or technical retention leaves plan content, transcripts, interpretations, or audio behind, or erasing them deletes applied business work.
A transcription whose outcome may have been charged is resent, or its charge is lost, so usage is double-counted or unbounded.

A calendar mirror, capacity reservation, or other plan input committed after Apply rechecked the day but before it committed (including a new meeting or reservation the plan could not lock) leaves an applied plan resting on stale availability.
A transcription response is buffered without bound, or a clipped transcript is stored and offered as complete, so different words are saved or interpreted as if they were what was said.
